tools.description:
Launch a new agent to handle complex, multi-step tasks. Each agent type has specific capabilities and tools available to it.

Available agent types are listed in <system-reminder> messages in the conversation.

When using the Agent tool, specify a subagent_type to select an agent: `"fork"` forks yourself (the fork inherits your full conversation context and always runs on your model — a `model` override is ignored); any other type — or omitting it — starts a fresh agent (general-purpose by default).

## When to use

A fresh agent costs more than it looks. It knows only what you put in the prompt, and you see only the summary it sends back — both handoffs drop detail, and neither of you can tell what the other missed. You can't watch it work, only wait or cancel. Its mistakes come back in the same confident register as its findings, and an agent handed your hypothesis tends to return it confirmed. Several at once spend tokens in a burst the user didn't ask for. Weigh those tokens against the accuracy they buy: the user pays for agents you did not need, and pays again for work you redo because you skipped one.

Reach for this when you have independent work to run in parallel, when the user asks for a side quest that shouldn't block your main thread, or when answering would mean reading across several files — delegate that and you keep the conclusion, not the file dumps.

Do the work yourself when it is a handful of tool calls or a lookup whose target you already know; don't delegate a check you could run inline. Delegate review only when you want a read that isn't anchored on yours — then give it the code, not your conclusion. Once you've delegated something, don't also run it yourself; wait for the result. When in doubt, don't spawn.

When you do spawn one, brief it like the peer it is: state the goal and what you have already ruled out, point it at the files and docs worth reading instead of retyping them, and keep the scope explicit and narrow. That brief is the only context it will have, so it is your first lever on every cost above — and if you cannot write a clear one, you do not understand the task well enough to hand it off.

A fork keeps its tool output out of your context. If you are the fork, execute directly — don't re-delegate.

- The agent's final report is not shown to the user — relay what matters.
- Use SendMessage with the agent's ID or name to continue a previously spawned agent with its context intact; a new Agent call starts fresh (except subagent_type: "fork", which inherits your context).
- Each agent type's model, reasoning effort, and tools come from its definition (`.claude/agents/*.md` frontmatter or SDK `agents`).
- `isolation: "worktree"` gives the agent its own git worktree (auto-cleaned if unchanged).
- Subagents run in the background by default; you'll be notified when one completes. Pass `run_in_background: false` only when your very next action depends on the result and nothing else could usefully happen while it runs — otherwise background it so the user can interject. Never fabricate or predict a pending agent's results — the notification is never something you write yourself; if the user asks before it arrives, say it's still running.

1	# kitty — shared trip expenses CLI: design
2	
3	Status: draft for approval · 2026-11-17
4	
5	## Intent
6	
7	A small command-line tool for tracking shared expenses on group trips and
8	working out who owes whom at the end. It will be reused across many trips
9	and groups, one `kitty.json` per trip folder. Nothing exotic, but **the
10	numbers must be exactly right and identical every time** — same inputs,
11	same outputs, no float drift, no results that shift after later changes.
12	
13	## Goals
14	
15	- Record members, expenses (with flexible splits and foreign currencies),
16	  and repayments.
17	- Report balances, a settle-up plan, per-person history, and per-category
18	  spending as JSON that is stable enough to script against.
19	- Export expenses to CSV.
20	- Clean errors: message + exit status 1, never a traceback.
21	
22	## Non-goals
23	
24	- Multiple kitties per file, multi-user sync, online exchange rates,
25	  editing expenses in place (remove and re-add instead), payment removal,
26	  pretty/table output.
27	
28	## Anti-goals (failure even if it "works")
29	
30	- Any floating-point arithmetic on money or rates.
31	- Re-deriving old splits or conversions from current state (current rates,
32	  current members) — history must be frozen when recorded.
33	- Non-deterministic output (ordering, tie-breaking, rounding).
34	
35	## Constraints
36	
37	- Python 3.9.6 (installed) — no `match`, no runtime `X | Y` unions.
38	- Standard library only. Run as `python3 -m kitty <command>` from the
39	  project folder.
40	- Data lives in `./kitty.json` (current working directory).
41	- Tests with `unittest`.
42	
43	## Approaches considered
44	
45	1. **Small package with separated layers** — `money`, `store`, `ledger`,
46	   `cli` modules; integer cents and `Decimal` rates. Each rule (rounding,
47	   splitting, settling) is unit-testable on its own. **Chosen** by the
48	   user: the risk in this tool is in the money rules, and this isolates
49	   them.
50	2. Single `__main__.py` — quicker to read initially, but mixes argument
51	   parsing with the arithmetic and gets harder to test as ~15 commands
52	   accumulate.
53	3. Class-heavy domain model (Expense/Payment/Member objects with
54	   persistence) — mostly boilerplate for a JSON file plus arithmetic.
55	
56	Rejected outright: floats for money; storing only raw inputs and
57	recomputing splits at report time.
58	
59	## Package layout
60	
61	```
62	kitty/
63	  __init__.py
64	  __main__.py   # calls cli.main()
65	  money.py      # parse/format cents, parse rates, convert, allocate
66	  store.py      # load/save kitty.json, schema, atomic write
67	  ledger.py     # balances, settle, history, report, CSV rows
68	  cli.py        # argparse commands, KittyError -> "error: ..." + exit 1
69	tests/
70	  test_money.py, test_ledger.py, test_cli.py
71	```
72	
73	A single exception type `KittyError` (in `money.py` or its own module) is
74	raised for every user-facing error; `cli.main()` catches it, prints
75	`error: <message>` to stderr, exits 1. argparse usage errors must also
76	exit 1 (override `ArgumentParser.error`), not argparse's default 2.
77	
78	## Money rules (decided by the user unless marked)
79	
80	- **Representation:** all money is stored and computed as integer cents.
81	  Rates are stored as exact decimal strings and handled with `Decimal`.
82	- **Formatting:** strings with exactly two decimals, `-` for negatives
83	  (e.g. `-0.05`, `20.70`, `0.00`).
84	- **Conversion (builder/assistant call):** `base_cents = amount_cents ×
85	  rate`, rounded half-up to a whole cent (`Decimal` `ROUND_HALF_UP`).
86	  Base currency rate is implicitly 1. Using a currency with no rate set is
87	  an error.
88	- **Rates are frozen per entry (user):** each expense and payment stores
89	  the rate in effect when it was added. `rate set` only affects later
90	  entries.
91	- **Splitting (user):** split happens in base-currency cents after
92	  conversion. Each participant gets their portion rounded down; the
93	  leftover cents go one each to participants in order. Order is the order
94	  listed in `--among` / `--shares` / `--percent` / `--exact`, or member
95	  join order when splitting among everyone. Example: 10.00 among Alice,
96	  Bob, Cara → 3.34, 3.33, 3.33.
97	  - Implemented as weighted allocation: share_i = ⌊total × w_i / W⌋, then
98	    leftover cents (always fewer than the number of participants) one each
99	    in order. Equal split: all weights 1. Shares: the given numbers.
100	    Percent: the given percentages.
101	- **`--exact` (agreed):** amounts are in the expense's own currency and
102	  must sum exactly to the expense amount. The base total is converted
103	  once, then allocated using the exact amounts as weights with the rule
104	  above, so shares always sum to `base_amount`. In base currency this
105	  yields exactly the typed amounts.
106	- **Shares are frozen per expense (agreed):** computed at `expense add` and
107	  stored. Members added later don't join old splits.
108	- **Invariant:** for every expense, shares sum to its base amount; all
109	  balances sum to zero.
110	
111	## Data file (`kitty.json`) — builder may refine field names
112	
113	```json
114	{
115	  "version": 1,
116	  "base_currency": "EUR",
117	  "members": ["Alice", "Bob"],
118	  "rates": {"USD": "0.92"},
119	  "next_id": 2,
120	  "next_seq": 3,
121	  "expenses": [
122	    {"id": 1, "seq": 1, "date": "2026-07-14", "payer": "Alice",
123	     "description": "Dinner", "amount_cents": 4500, "currency": "USD",
124	     "rate": "0.92", "base_cents": 4140, "category": "food",
125	     "shares": [["Alice", 2070], ["Bob", 2070]]}
126	  ],
127	  "payments": [
128	    {"seq": 2, "date": "2026-07-15", "from": "Bob", "to": "Alice",
129	     "amount_cents": 2070, "currency": "EUR", "rate": "1",
130	     "base_cents": 2070}
131	  ]
132	}
133	```
134	
135	- `seq` is a global counter across expenses and payments, recording the
136	  order things were added (for tie-breaking in `history`).
137	- Expense IDs are never reused (`next_id` only grows), even after removal.
138	- Shares stored as an ordered list of pairs to preserve split order.
139	- Saves are atomic: write a temp file in the same directory, then
140	  `os.replace`.
141	- Missing file (any command but `init`), unreadable/invalid JSON → error.
142	
143	## Commands
144	
145	Output: reporting commands print JSON (`json.dumps`, insertion order
146	preserved) to stdout. Mutating commands print nothing on success, except
147	`expense add`, which prints the new ID as a bare number (assistant call).
148	
149	| Command | Behaviour |
150	|---|---|
151	| `init CUR` | Create `kitty.json` with base currency CUR. Error if it already exists. |
152	| `member add NAME` | Append to members (join order). |
153	| `member remove NAME` | Error if NAME appears anywhere — as payer, sharer, payment sender or recipient. Otherwise remove. (user) |
154	| `member list` | `["Alice", "Bob"]` in join order. |
155	| `expense add PAYER AMOUNT DESCRIPTION [--among A,B \| --exact A=30,B=20 \| --shares A=2,B=1 \| --percent A=60,B=40] [--currency CUR] [--date YYYY-MM-DD] [--category CAT]` | Default: equal among all current members, base currency, today (local date), category `other`. The four split options are mutually exclusive. Prints new ID. |
156	| `expense list` | Array ordered by ID, shape below. |
157	| `expense remove ID` | Error if no such ID. |
158	| `payment add FROM TO AMOUNT [--currency CUR] [--date D]` | FROM's balance goes up, TO's goes down, by the base amount. |
159	| `rate set CUR RATE` | 1 CUR = RATE base. Overwrites earlier value for future entries only. |
160	| `balances` | Object of every current member (join order), including `"0.00"`. |
161	| `settle` | Array of suggested payments (rules below). `[]` if all square. |
162	| `history NAME` | Array of entries affecting NAME with running balance. |
163	| `report` | Per-category, per-person sum of shares. |
164	| `export FILE` | Write CSV, overwriting FILE. |
165	
166	Output shapes (from the user):

tools.description:
Launch a new agent to handle complex, multi-step tasks. Each agent type has specific capabilities and tools available to it.

Available agent types are listed in <system-reminder> messages in the conversation.

When using the Agent tool, specify a subagent_type to select an agent: `"fork"` forks yourself (the fork inherits your full conversation context and always runs on your model — a `model` override is ignored); any other type — or omitting it — starts a fresh agent (general-purpose by default).

## When to use

A fresh agent costs more than it looks. It knows only what you put in the prompt, and you see only the summary it sends back — both handoffs drop detail, and neither of you can tell what the other missed. You can't watch it work, only wait or cancel. Its mistakes come back in the same confident register as its findings, and an agent handed your hypothesis tends to return it confirmed. Several at once spend tokens in a burst the user didn't ask for. Weigh those tokens against the accuracy they buy: the user pays for agents you did not need, and pays again for work you redo because you skipped one.

Reach for this when you have independent work to run in parallel, when the user asks for a side quest that shouldn't block your main thread, or when answering would mean reading across several files — delegate that and you keep the conclusion, not the file dumps.

Do the work yourself when it is a handful of tool calls or a lookup whose target you already know; don't delegate a check you could run inline. Delegate review only when you want a read that isn't anchored on yours — then give it the code, not your conclusion. Once you've delegated something, don't also run it yourself; wait for the result. When in doubt, don't spawn.

When you do spawn one, brief it like the peer it is: state the goal and what you have already ruled out, point it at the files and docs worth reading instead of retyping them, and keep the scope explicit and narrow. That brief is the only context it will have, so it is your first lever on every cost above — and if you cannot write a clear one, you do not understand the task well enough to hand it off.

A fork keeps its tool output out of your context. If you are the fork, execute directly — don't re-delegate.

- The agent's final report is not shown to the user — relay what matters.
- Use SendMessage with the agent's ID or name to continue a previously spawned agent with its context intact; a new Agent call starts fresh (except subagent_type: "fork", which inherits your context).
- Each agent type's model, reasoning effort, and tools come from its definition (`.claude/agents/*.md` frontmatter or SDK `agents`).
- `isolation: "worktree"` gives the agent its own git worktree (auto-cleaned if unchanged).
- Subagents run in the background by default; you'll be notified when one completes. Pass `run_in_background: false` only when your very next action depends on the result and nothing else could usefully happen while it runs — otherwise background it so the user can interject. Never fabricate or predict a pending agent's results — the notification is never something you write yourself; if the user asks before it arrives, say it's still running.
